Mindaugas's kingship relied on relatives, partners and local leaders whose relations were affected by baptism and alliances. Kin could mediate but also compete over land and standing. Beyond public promises, actual troops and supplies showed whose support was effective. Kin disputes changed commands and musters, requiring retainers to know whom to follow. Familiarity did not ensure safe routes, and treatment of relatives and captives affected service.

Marriages and land grants won support but could anger other heirs; public or written promises needed witnesses and fulfillment.
